sentences.text: Cryolophosaurus possessed a unique nasal crest that ran over the eyes, rose perpendicular to the skull, and fanned out.
Subadult individuals were estimated to be 6 to 7 meters long and weigh between 350 and 465 kilograms, while larger adults reached a length of 8 meters.
This animal was a large, robust theropod and one of the largest of its time.
Due to the strange crest on its forehead, Cryolophosaurus is popularly known as Elvisaurus, resembling the hairstyle of rock artist Elvis Presley.
Based on length and weight estimates, Cryolophosaurus is currently the largest known early Jurassic theropod.
Cryolophosaurus is the first theropod found in Antarctica and possibly one of the oldest known tetanurans.
Paleontologist Dr. William Hammer first excavated Cryolophosaurus in 1991 from the Early Jurassic Hanson Formation in Antarctica.
The genus Cryolophosaurus was described by Hammer & Hickerson in 1994.
New Cryolophosaurus material was unearthed in Antarctica in 2013, though its full description remains unpublished.
The discovery of long cervical ribs in the mouth of the type specimen led researchers to hypothesize that Cryolophosaurus was feeding on a prosauropod when it died.
Hammer concluded that a post-canine tooth from a tritylodont was part of the stomach contents of the Cryolophosaurus specimen when it died.
Hammer suggested that the Cryolophosaurus individual might have drowned because the prosauropod ribs extended into the theropod's neck region.
Pathologies in some Cryolophosaurus bones provide evidence of scavenging behavior.
Rootless broken teeth from a juvenile Cryolophosaurus found nearby suggest they shed naturally while scavenging an adult carcass.
Pathologies found on some Cryolophosaurus bones show evidence of scavenging behavior.
Broken teeth from at least two different theropods have been found near Cryolophosaurus fossils.
Research found the fossil has an almost complete, undistorted cranial cavity sufficient to approximate the shape and size of the living brain.
The brain of Cryolophosaurus was more primitive compared to other theropods.
Studies suggest the distinctive crest of Cryolophosaurus was used for intra-species recognition.
Thomas R. Holtz Jr. discovered in 2010 that the strange crest of Cryolophosaurus served primarily for intraspecific recognition based on related species evidence and bone texture studies.
Cryolophosaurus is currently classified as a derived neotheropod closely related to Averostra.
A 2020 study by Adam Marsh and Timothy Rowe classified Cryolophosaurus as a basal neotheropod.

Cryolophosaurus ellioti is the only known species of the extinct Cryolophosaurus genus, a basal dilophosaurid theropod that lived during the Early Jurassic, approximately 186 to 182 million years ago, in what is now Antarctica.
Cryolophosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic Period, approximately 196 to 188 million years ago.
Cryolophosaurus fossils were found about 650 km from the South Pole, which was approximately 1000 km farther north during the time the animal lived.
The classification of Cryolophosaurus remains debated due to its mix of primitive and advanced characteristics.
However, new studies in 2007 demonstrated Cryolophosaurus was probably a ceratosaurian more closely related to Dilophosaurus and Dracovenator than to tetanurans.
Researchers challenged the idea that the bizarre crest and armor of Cryolophosaurus were primarily for mating, fighting rivals, or intimidating predators.
In 2019, the species recognition function of the crest was disputed, while a socio-sexual display model was suggested.
